porcelain.summary: Missing dated Zhou prevalence event accepted; duplicate Shang event rejected.
questions: Can original archaeological site reports independently clarify locations, chronology and meaning of wider prevalence?
Would a later schema explicitly representing spread better capture a general change in prevalence without implying a named receiving community?
limitations: An abstract-level assertion; not a site-by-site demonstration or a new independent corroborating source.
This is a proposal, not an independent review; existing research basis is not upgraded.
A separate source record preserves the existing shared source file while citing the same author and abstract; it is not independent evidence.

jikji.summary: Earlier reported Goryeo metal-type edition accepted; direct lineage to Jikji remains unestablished.
questions: Inspect and translate the original postface and establish early manuscript witnesses and dating.
Find independently informative evidence, if it exists, identifying a technical or organizational lineage to the 1377 Jikji edition.
limitations: The original Korean historical witness was not directly inspected. Both secondary accounts rely on historical literature; they are not independent evidence of transmission. No date or invention priority is claimed outside the explicitly estimated range.
Yoo and Yun dispute conventional interpretation of a separate Song of Enlightenment edition; those claims were not evaluated or adopted.

newcomen.summary: Savery published description and Newcomen adoption bound accepted; influence and successful Savery mine installation remain unresolved.
questions: Did Savery’s engine or its technical ideas directly influence Newcomen’s development? Need independently informative sources and precise relation; chronological similarity alone is insufficient.
Where and when were early Savery engines actually installed and operated?
What is the underlying evidence and geographic distribution for the museum’s count of at least 100 engines by 1729?

antikythera.summary: Existing event extended with eclipse-dial details; Babylonian relationship remains a candidate question.
questions: Find independent informative evidence of any specific transmission of Saros/eclipse theory into the mechanism, and distinguish shared cycle from direct influence.
Date earlier geared devices from original ancient witnesses and archaeology; construction date of this artefact is not the first gears.
Investigate subsequent uptake or disappearance independently; no loss or abandonment is inferred from catalogue gaps.

Nonblocking inherited issue: assess competing palaeographic evidence for construction date. Freeth infers 150–100 BCE from lettering, while Iversen and Jones discuss forms occurring across a wider late-third to mid-first century BCE interval. Reconsider the old date and source attribution without treating publication date, wreck date, or an observed astronomical epoch as a direct age. Neither its basis nor its old claim is upgraded by this review.
Investigate transmission and later uptake separately: matching cycles and absent descendants prove neither a specific route nor loss.

nodes.name: Sangjeong Gogeum Yemun metal-type edition
nodes.description: A Goryeo metal-type printing of Sangjeong Gogeum Yemun is recorded in a postface; the museum account reports 28 copies.

date.label: estimated 1234–1241
date.basis: Yoo and Yun estimate 1234–1241 from historical literature. The museum dates the postface around 1234; neither provides an inspected dated edition in this lane.

nodes.caveats: The record is a reported edition, not the origin of metal type or evidence that its particular types or methods passed to the Jikji printers.

nodes.name: Savery’s fire engine for raising water
nodes.description: Savery described a water-raising engine using steam condensation to draw water into a vessel and steam pressure to force it out.

date.basis: Publication year on the title page of the source transcription.

nodes.caveats: The account is the inventor’s own promotional description; this record does not establish influence on Newcomen or an actual mine installation.

date.label: estimated 1234–1241
date.basis: Yoo and Yun estimate 1234–1241 from historical literature. The museum dates the postface around 1234; neither provides an inspected dated edition in this lane.

event.statement: A postface records printing 28 copies using movable metal type; a secondary synthesis estimates the printing at 1234–1241.
event.caveats: The printed copies have not been found according to Yoo and Yun. The postface itself was not inspected in the original language; date is an estimate. No direction of technological transmission to the Jikji edition is established.

evidence.supports: Museum describes a postface recording 28 copies printed with movable metal type in Goryeo.
A secondary synthesis estimates printing between 1234 and 1241 and notes no copies found.

date.label: by 1729
date.basis: The museum dates the reported minimum count to the time of Newcomen’s death in 1729.

event.statement: By 1729, at least 100 Newcomen engines were in use across Europe, according to National Museums Scotland.
event.scope: Use of the engine type across Europe; the museum does not enumerate sites or dates of individual installations.
event.caveats: The count is a museum synthesis, not a directly inspected contemporary register; this is not an invention date.

evidence.supports: Museum reports at least 100 engines of the type in use across Europe by Newcomen’s death in 1729.

events.record_name: Savery’s fire engine for raising water

date.basis: Publication year on the title page of the source transcription.

event.statement: In The Miner’s Friend, Savery described a fire-driven water-raising engine using condensation and steam pressure.
event.caveats: This is the date of the published description, not the date of invention or proof of a successful mine installation.

evidence.locator: Title page; Chapter First, Manner of Working the Engine
evidence.supports: Publication year and operating description: steam condenses, water rises into a vessel, and steam pressure forces it out.

date.label: Zhou dynasty, 1027–221 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it; the period bounds do not date the onset of wider prevalence more precisely.

event.statement: Proto-porcelain became more widespread during the Zhou dynasty, 1027 to 221 BCE.

evidence.supports: Proto-porcelain became more widespread during the subsequent Zhou dynasty (1027 to 221 BC).

event_extensions.record_name: Toothed gearing in the Hellenistic Greek world

date.label: around the end of the 2nd century BC
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

event.statement: The Antikythera Mechanism, a Greek geared device, was constructed around the end of the second century BC; it is evidence that gear trains existed by then, not a date for the first gears. Its eclipse dial represented a 223-lunar-month cycle and marked possible solar or lunar eclipses; about one third of the scale survives.

evidence.supports: constructed around the end of the second century bc
The spiral scale represents 223 lunar months, includes eclipse-possibility glyphs, and is about one third extant.

date.label: around the end of the 2nd century BC
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

before.statement: The Antikythera Mechanism, a Greek geared device, was constructed around the end of the second century BC; it is evidence that gear trains existed by then, not a date for the first gears.

edge.statement: Did the eclipse scheme represented on the Antikythera Mechanism draw on Babylonian astronomical methods involving the 223-month Saros?
edge.scope: The eclipse dial only; a shared cycle does not itself establish how or from whom knowledge reached the makers.

evidence.supports: The dial represents a 223-month cycle with eclipse-possibility glyphs.
Late Babylonian astronomy used the 223-synodic-month Saros for eclipse possibilities.
